title: The Streams Underfoot
gist: Morocco, after seven years of drought, still has hundreds of active khettaras, ancient gravity-fed underground water tunnels, which cost far less to run than pumped wells but are neglected by officials who favor drip irrigation and pumps. The piece argues qanats are a sustainable, overlooked tool as droughts rise worldwide.

insights.claim: Morocco endured seven consecutive drought years starting in 2018; the 2024 wheat harvest fell by half, and only rains in winter 2025-26 partially recharged aquifers.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Morocco's agricultural output is highly drought-exposed; watch food-import demand and rainfall.
insights.locator: The Kingdom of Morocco is accustomed to dealing with water scarcity

insights.claim: Desalination in Morocco, including Africa's largest commercial plant near Agadir built by Spanish firm Coxabengoa, is energy-hungry, harms marine ecosystems via hypersaline discharge, meets under one-hundredth of national water needs and serves cities rather than farmers.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Desalination does not solve agricultural water demand, limiting its role in food security.
insights.locator: One high-tech strategy for coping with water scarcity

insights.claim: Geographer Dale Lightfoot inventoried 90,000 qanats across about 20 countries, 46,000 still supplying water, some operating continuously for 2,300 years; as much as half of Iran's irrigated land relies on them.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Qanats remain material infrastructure in arid economies, notably Iran.

insights.claim: A qanat is a gently sloped hand-dug tunnel that collects water from an aquifer by gravity, so it flows continuously without depleting the aquifer and loses little water to evaporation.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Gravity-fed designs have near-zero energy cost and sustainable extraction.
insights.quote: Qanats flow continuously yet do not diminish the aquifer
insights.locator: The principle behind the qanat is simple

insights.claim: Diesel-powered pump wells can exhaust fossil groundwater in months, and farmers pumping for watermelons and argan trees drain aquifers, making land useless and accelerating rural exodus to cities.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Groundwater depletion from cash crops is a stranded-asset and rural-stability risk.
insights.locator: Like a vertical straw plunged into an aquifer

insights.claim: Qanats are typically five times cheaper to operate than a pumped well, though a five-mile tunnel at 45 feet depth may cost $1 million by hand, with the investment recouped after about 30 years.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Long payback and high up-front labor explain underinvestment despite low lifetime costs.
insights.locator: In the long term, traditional systems are a great investment

insights.claim: Archaeologist Emily Hayes-Rich estimates Morocco has 2,400 khettaras, about 350 still active and some newly built or concrete-reinforced, contradicting officials who call them abandoned relics.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Official statistics may undercount community-managed infrastructure.

insights.claim: Moroccan regional agricultural offices subsidize drip irrigation fed by pumped groundwater, which lowers water tables and undermines khettaras that depend on rainfall and snowmelt, according to hydrologist Abdennabi El Mandour.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Subsidy design for water-saving tech can accelerate aquifer depletion; watch agri-tech subsidy winners.
insights.locator: The state, he explains, favors reimbursing small farmers

insights.claim: Hassan II's 1960s megadam program aimed to make a million acres of desert arable and keep usable water from reaching the sea, greening the north but not the arid southwest.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Historical capital allocation favored dams over local systems.

insights.claim: The incidence of droughts worldwide has risen 29% since the start of the 21st century, and megacities including Jakarta, Mexico City, Sao Paulo, Chennai, Tehran and Cairo have faced Day Zero scenarios.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Structural rise in water-stress exposure supports demand for water infrastructure and efficiency.
insights.locator: Since the beginning of the 21st century
